paras: The Plymouth riot of 1881 was a series of clashes in Plymouth, North Carolina, in late December 1881, in which armed Black residents were reported to have shot a constable, killed a member of his posse and rescued prisoners from the sheriff. After the mayor telegraphed that 300 armed men were defying the law, Gov. Jarvis sent militia, and a sheriff's posse restored order with at least five arrests on December 30. Papers across the country carried the story as a 'negro riot', and North Carolina editors held it up as proof of the Governor's resolve.

Plymouth, a town of about 1,200 people with a large Black majority, lay across the sound some twenty miles from Edenton and had no telegraph line. A Raleigh informant quoted by the Richmond Dispatch described the Black laborers who cut lumber and staves in the nearby woods and swamps as 'a rough lot, given to fighting', especially on holidays.

According to W. D. Pruden of Edenton, writing to the Raleigh News and Observer on the word of a steamer captain and the mayor's messenger, a fight broke out among Black men at Plymouth on Saturday, December 24. The constable who tried to stop it was beaten and shot, one of his posse, later named as Mr. Butler, was mortally wounded, and another was stabbed.

On Tuesday several men were arrested and bound over to the Superior Court, but a crowd attacked the sheriff on the way to jail and freed them. Dr. Woodson, who was attending the dying man, was also attacked but not seriously hurt, and Matt. Wilson was named as the leader. On the morning of December 29 Mayor A. D. Gaylord telegraphed that 'there are 300 negroes here, defying the law all around, with guns', and asked for troops.

Gov. Jarvis ordered Lieut. Col. John W. Cotton and two companies to Plymouth, the Pasquotank Rifles of Elizabeth City were accepted, and the Edgecombe Guards left Tarboro. The troops arrived on December 30, and Sheriff Dempsey Spruill with an armed posse restored quiet, sending five prisoners to jail at Edenton. The Governor, arriving that afternoon, reported four men wounded on Saturday, one since dead, and said the posse had made its arrests before the troops came.

The rioters were said to have fled to the swamps, the troops were to return at once, and the 'murderer of Mr. Butler' was reported still at large. A Charlotte paper expected a prompt trial, but no report of one appears in the coverage.

The Norfolk wire first reported a 'threatening riot' on December 28 and 29, and by December 30 and 31 papers from Memphis to Chicago, Omaha and Cheyenne carried the mayor's telegram and the troop movements. Headlines leaned on race and alarm: the Lancaster Intelligencer wrote of 'Dastardly Doings', and the Omaha Bee ran 'BLOODY BLACKS' with a claim that the troops would 'have no scruple about firing into them'.

North Carolina and Georgia papers turned the story into praise for Gov. Jarvis, the Savannah Morning News saying that under a less decisive governor the riot 'might have assumed ugly proportions'. The Orange County Observer reprinted the account 'as a warning to all others', and the Milton Chronicle wrote that the ringleaders 'should be hanged as high as old John Brown'.

The only Black voice in the coverage was a letter signed 'Colored Republican' in the Goldsboro Star, which did not excuse violence against officers but held that whiskey caused the riot and that the officer 'very likely' approached the rioters 'in a rash manner'. The writer set Plymouth beside the lynching of two Black prisoners at Oxford, about which, the letter said, nothing had been said.

A Raleigh special to the Chicago Tribune traced the trouble to the arrest of Jake Slinger, a popular Black local politician, on a Christmas spree, and the Omaha Bee spoke of a mob seeking to free 'Jake Stinger' under a leader named Dick Hickens. Casualty figures differed as well: the Omaha Bee reported four wounded white men denied doctors, and a rumor that Sheriff Spruill had been badly hurt and a Black man killed was printed as 'not well authenticated'.

reader.title: Plymouth riot of 1881
bases: Every account describes armed Black residents resisting arrest, shooting a constable, killing a posse member and rescuing prisoners, met by a sheriff's posse and state militia that made arrests; no confirmed violence by whites against Black people is reported beyond an unauthenticated rumor (A6, A9, A13, A20).

The Edenton/News and Observer account, the mayor's telegram, the Governor's report and independent Raleigh specials agree on the core riot, rescue and militia response (A1, A13, A15, A20), though details of cause, leader and casualties differ.

accounts.gist: Black men fighting among themselves resisted, beat and shot the constable, mortally wounded one posse member and stabbed another; on Tuesday a mob rescued prisoners from the sheriff.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Raleigh special
accounts.gist: The trouble began with the arrest of Jake Slinger, a popular Black politician, on a Christmas spree; crowds gathered to force the jail and free him.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee Raleigh dispatches
accounts.gist: An armed Black mob held the town, threatened to tear down the jail to rescue Jake Stinger, built a barricade with an old cannon under Dick Hickens, and had wounded four white men.

accounts.label: Governor's report
accounts.gist: Four men were wounded in Saturday's fighting, one has died; the sheriff's posse made the arrests before the troops arrived.

accounts.label: Colored Republican letter
accounts.gist: Whiskey caused the riot, and the officer very likely approached the rioters rashly; violence against officers should still be punished.

framing.detail: Most papers outside the state ran the Norfolk and Raleigh wires on the mayor's telegram and the troops under headlines such as 'Serious Riot—Sheriff Attacked by Negroes' and 'THE PLYMOUTH MOB'.
The Omaha Bee headlined 'BLOODY BLACKS' and reported the troops would 'have no scruple about firing into them'; Lancaster called it 'Dastardly Doings'.
North Carolina and Savannah editors praised Gov. Jarvis's promptness as a warning to 'lawless bands', and the Milton Chronicle called for the ringleaders to be hanged.
The 'Colored Republican' letter condemned violence against officers but blamed whiskey and a rash officer and pointed to unpunished lynching.

info: Initial fight and shooting of the constable on Saturday (Dec. 24); prisoners rescued from the sheriff on Tuesday (Dec. 27); mayor telegraphed for troops on Dec. 29; troops arrived and quiet was restored Dec. 30.
Plymouth, N.C., a town on the sound about twenty miles across from Edenton, with no telegraph line.

The town constable (unnamed) was beaten and shot; Mr. Butler, a member of his posse, was mortally wounded and later reported dead; another posse member was stabbed; Dr. Woodson was attacked but not seriously hurt; Sheriff Spruill was attacked during the rescue.
Black men were accused of shooting the constable while resisting arrest for a breach of the peace, killing Mr. Butler, and rescuing prisoners from the sheriff.

In the dominant account, armed Black residents and laborers from the shingle swamps; Matt. Wilson named as leader by the Edenton report, Dick Hickens by an Omaha-printed Raleigh dispatch. The force used against the rioters was Sheriff Dempsey Spruill's posse and state militia.
A rumor that a negro had been killed was reported as not well authenticated; no later report confirms it.
Quiet restored Dec. 30; rioters said to have fled to nearby swamps; trial expected when a court could convene. No report of a trial was found.
